subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

section_titles: Equal sharing and the concept of half
periods.activity_title: Folding Fair: Discovering What a Half Means

tasks_in_class.description: How do you share objects equally?
Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?
Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half. Find all the different ways to make a half. Repeat with a square piece of paper.
Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.

time_bands.activity: Open with Let us Discuss Q1, p.107 ("How do you share objects equally?") — pairs of children mime sharing a piece of bread, a bundle of pencils, a length of ribbon; the class hears what 'equal' means in their own words before any written form is shown.

Move to Let us Discuss Q2, p.107 ("Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?") — each child folds their own rectangular sheet of paper so one part sits exactly on the other; class notices the two parts match, names this a 'half', and articulates why folding reveals equal sharing.

Children continue with Let us Explore, p.110 ("Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half....") — they try every fold they can find for the rectangle, then repeat with a square, and share the different fold-lines found; the class collects evidence that a whole can be halved in more than one way.

Close with Let us Do Q1, p.108 ("Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.") — children apply the fold-based understanding to pictorial shapes, justifying each choice aloud or in writing.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often think that 'half' means any split into two pieces rather than two equal pieces; prompt them to overlay the two parts to check. Additional pictorial practice is available in Let us Do Q2 and Q3 (pp.108–109) for children who finish quickly. Materials for folding should be paper rectangles and squares each child keeps for reference.
materials: rectangular sheets of paper (one per child)
square sheets of paper (one per child)

section_titles: Equal sharing and the concept of half
periods.activity_title: Drawing, Colouring and Completing the Half

tasks_in_class.description: Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.
Draw lines to show different ways of making a half.
Complete the whole picture by drawing the other half.
Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair? Is there another fair way?

homework.description: Here are some mangoes. Share them equally between the two children.

time_bands.activity: Children open their books to Let us Do Q2, p.108 ("Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.") — they draw the dividing line on each shape, then compare lines with a neighbour to see whether different lines can still make equal halves.

Move to Let us Do Q5, p.109 ("Draw lines to show different ways of making a half.") — children record every valid half-line they can find on each shape, building the idea that a half is defined by equality of parts, not by the direction of the line.

Let us Do Q6, p.109 ("Complete the whole picture by drawing the other half.") — children use the given half as a mirror guide and draw the missing half; pairs check each other's work by folding or by visual comparison.

Close with Let us Discuss, p.110 ("Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair? Is there another fair way?") — brief whole-class conversation about whether physical objects that cannot be cut can still be shared fairly, consolidating equal-sharing reasoning beyond shape-folding.

periods.teacher_notes: Children drawing the 'other half' sometimes produce a rough mirror image that does not match; encourage them to fold the paper to check. Let us Do Q3 and Q4 (p.109) on the chikki context are available as additional practice for fast finishers. Assign Let us Do, p.110 (sharing mangoes) as take-home reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Marble Counts: Half and Double on the Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8; 8 marbles are ___ of 4; 10 marbles are ___ of 5; 5 marbles are ___ of 10; 6 marbles are ___ of 12; 12 marbles are ___ of 6.
On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the marble-sharing story from the Half and Double section; draw a 0–17 number line on the board together with the class. Pairs of children call out a number, its half, and its double, locating all three on the shared line — building a visual stock of half-and-double pairs before any written task.

Children complete Fill in blanks, p.111 ("Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8; 8 marbles are ___ of 4....") — each blank is answered and checked against the number line on the board, reinforcing the inverse relationship between halving and doubling through a concrete number-line anchor.

Move to Number line, p.111 ("On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?") — children locate each value on their own drawn number line, count the gap, and write the distance; two or three children explain their counting strategy to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is swapping half and double — children write 'half of 4 is 8' rather than 'double of 4 is 8'; pause after the first blank-filling pair and ask the class to justify which word is larger. The number line (0–17) from p.111 is the section's pictorial model and should remain visible throughout this unit.

periods.activity_title: Guess Who I Am: Puzzles with Half and Double

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112
tasks_in_class.description: I have less than the double of 3 marbles and more than the half of 8 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 4, (b) 5, (c) 6 marbles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q2, p.112
tasks_in_class.description: I have less than the double of 4 marbles and more than the half of 10 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 8, (b) 6, (c) 3 marbles.

time_bands.activity: Warm up by calling out number-pairs and asking children to state both the half and the double quickly — this oral round revisits the halving-and-doubling relationship from the fill-in-the-blanks work and readies the class for constraint-based reasoning.

Children work through Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112 ("I have less than the double of 3 marbles and more than the half of 8 marbles....") — they first compute each boundary, mark both on a number line, and then identify which of the three options falls between the boundaries before ticking.

Children work through Guess Who am I? Q2, p.112 ("I have less than the double of 4 marbles and more than the half of 10 marbles....") — same number-line strategy; small groups compare answers and explain why the other options are outside the stated range.
A brief whole-class share: one group poses their own 'Guess Who am I?' clue using half and double, and the class tries to solve it — extending the reasoning playfully.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often tick without computing the boundaries first; insist they write 'double of 3 = ___' and 'half of 8 = ___' before ticking, so the number line becomes the decision tool. Children who find the puzzles straightforward can pose their own two-clue mystery-number for a partner to solve.

periods.activity_title: Four Equal Shares: Meeting the Quarter

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the objects that show quarters.
Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole (square, circle, flower, diamond).

time_bands.activity: Each child folds a square sheet of paper in half and then in half again; they open it and count the parts — four equal pieces, each called a quarter. The class discusses what happened: folding in half twice gives four equal shares, and each share is named 'one quarter'.

Children work through Let us Do Q1, p.113 ("Tick the objects that show quarters.") — they justify each tick or cross by explaining whether all four parts are equal, applying the fold-based definition to pictorial objects.

Children continue with Let us Do Q2, p.113 ("Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole (square, circle, flower, diamond).") — they try more than one valid set of lines for each shape where possible, and pairs compare to see that a quarter, like a half, can be shown in different ways.

periods.teacher_notes: Stress the term 'one quarter' rather than 'one out of four' from the outset, as the section's teacher note specifies. Children sometimes draw two parallel lines and call the resulting parts 'quarters' without checking equality; folding the printed shape after drawing can serve as a quick check.
materials: square sheets of paper (one per child)

periods.activity_title: Completing the Whole from a Quarter

tasks_in_class.description: Draw the remaining three quarters and complete the whole: (a) fan shape (b) striped rectangle.
Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole: (a) chocolate bar quarter (b) L-shaped quarter.

time_bands.activity: Quick oral round: the teacher holds up shapes folded to show one quarter and children say 'one quarter shown, three quarters hidden' — this anchors the language of missing parts before the drawing tasks begin.

Children work through Let us Do Q3, p.113 ("Draw the remaining three quarters and complete the whole: (a) fan shape (b) striped rectangle.") — they study the given quarter carefully and draw the three remaining parts so all four are equal; pairs check by folding or overlaying.

Children continue with Let us Do Q4, p.113 ("Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole: (a) chocolate bar quarter (b) L-shaped quarter.") — the L-shaped quarter is more demanding; the class discusses after completing it: how can an L-shape be a quarter of a whole?

periods.teacher_notes: The L-shaped quarter in Q4 often surprises children because they expect quarters to be regular triangles or rectangles; use this as an opportunity to reinforce that a quarter means one of four equal parts, regardless of the shape of each part. Encourage children to fold the completed whole to verify equality.

section_titles: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
periods.activity_title: From One Quarter to a Whole: Building Up

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the appropriate word (half/a quarter/double) to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.
Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.
Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.
Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the pictorial circle model from the section: draw 1 quarter → 2 quarters → 3 quarters → 4 quarters on the board, naming each stage aloud; children repeat the names chorally and notice that 2 quarters equals a half and 4 quarters equals a whole.

Children complete Half or Quarter?, p.114 ("Tick the appropriate word (half/a quarter/double) to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.") — this bridges all three terms introduced across the chapter and requires reasoning about part-whole relationships.

Children work through Let us Do Q1, p.115 ("Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.") and immediately follow with Let us Do Q2, p.115 ("Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters....") — colouring gives a concrete product that makes the progression from one to four quarters visible on the page.

Close with Let us Do Q4, p.116 ("Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.") — small groups discuss and then share one explanation with the class, reinforcing that quarters can appear in non-obvious partitions.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes count coloured sections without checking whether the parts are equal; ask 'Are all four parts the same size?' before accepting any colouring. Let us Do Q3, p.116 (drawing lines and colouring) is available as additional practice for children who finish quickly.

section_titles: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters

tasks_in_class.description: Draw lines and colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.
Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.
Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.

time_bands.activity: Children work through Let us Do Q3, p.116 ("Draw lines and colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters....") — they decide where to draw their own partition lines before colouring, making the drawing step explicit before the colouring step.

Children move to Let us Do Q5, p.116 ("Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.") — each child finds at least two different ways to shade a half and two different ways to shade a quarter on the same grid, sharing their designs with a neighbour and checking equality.

Children cut out the fraction cards from the book's perforated sheet and work on Let us Do Q6, p.116 ("Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.") — groups arrange quarter-cards until they form a complete whole, then try different arrangements; the class discusses what all successful arrangements have in common.

periods.teacher_notes: When children use the grid for Q5, they may shade any disconnected set of squares; guide them to check that the shaded region and the unshaded region each form equal parts of the whole grid. The fraction-card activity in Q6 is open-ended; accept any arrangement where four quarter-cards together cover the whole shape without overlap or gap.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Here is a square. Draw a line on it to show one half. Is there another way to draw the line? Draw that too.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any straight line that passes through the centre of the square and divides it into two equal parts is correct. Common valid lines include a horizontal line through the middle, a vertical line through the middle, and a diagonal line from corner to corner. Both drawings should show equal parts.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold (or mentally fold) the shape so one part sits exactly on the other — if the parts match, the line shows a half.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold the paper square first, then trace the fold-line; stretch: ask them to find a third different line that still makes a half.

exercise.description: Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Priya folded a rectangle in half in three different ways. Which fold makes two equal halves?

options.label: A
options.text: A fold that leaves one part empty

options.label: B
options.text: A fold that makes one piece bigger than the other

options.label: C
options.text: A fold that makes three pieces

options.label: D
options.text: A fold where one part sits exactly on top of the other

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A fold where one part sits exactly on top of the other — this means the two parts are equal, so each is a half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlay the two folded parts; if they match perfectly, the fold shows a half.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child thinks any division into two pieces is a half, without checking equality.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has confused halving with cutting into more than two pieces.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has not connected the idea of a half with two non-empty equal parts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold an actual rectangle and check; stretch: ask them to describe one more valid fold-line and explain why it still works.

exercise.description: Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half. Find all the different ways to make a half. Repeat with a square piece of paper.

items.prompt: Draw two lines on a square to cut it into four equal parts. Shade one part. What is that shaded part called?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two lines crossing at the centre (one horizontal, one vertical, or two diagonals) divide the square into four equal parts. The shaded part is called one quarter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the square in half and then in half again — the four equal parts each show one quarter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a paper square twice and trace the fold-lines before drawing; stretch: ask them to draw a different pair of lines that still gives four equal parts.

exercise.description: Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole (square, circle, flower, diamond).

items.prompt:
One quarter of a rectangle is shown below. Draw the remaining three quarters to complete the whole rectangle.
(Imagine a rectangle divided into four equal rows; only the top row is drawn.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The child draws three more sections of the same size and shape as the given quarter, arranged so the four parts together form one complete rectangle with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the given quarter as a template — copy its size and shape three times to fill the whole.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child trace the given quarter piece onto separate paper and physically place copies beside it; stretch: ask them to draw the whole in a different shape — for example, arranged in two rows of two instead of one row of four.

exercise.description: Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole: (a) chocolate bar quarter (b) L-shaped quarter.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Here is a grid with 8 squares arranged in 2 rows of 4. Shade the squares to show one half of the grid in two different ways.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two shadings each covering exactly 4 of the 8 squares are correct, provided the 4 shaded squares form one half. For example: shade the top row of 4; or shade the left 2 columns (4 squares); or shade any 4 squares that together equal half the grid. Two distinct shadings are required.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the total squares, find half that number, and shade exactly that many squares in two different arrangements.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: first count all 8 squares and write '4 is the half'; then shade any 4; stretch: ask the child to now shade one quarter of the same grid and explain how many squares that is.

exercise.description: Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Riya has four quarter-cards. She wants to arrange them to make one complete whole shape. Which arrangement will work?

options.label: A
options.text: Place all four cards together so they cover the whole shape with no gaps or overlaps

options.label: B
options.text: Place two cards side by side and leave the other two aside

options.label: C
options.text: Stack all four cards on top of each other

options.label: D
options.text: Use only one card because one quarter is enough for the whole

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Place all four cards together so they cover the whole shape with no gaps or overlaps — four quarters make one whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Four quarters together equal one whole: arrange all four cards so they fit together without gaps or overlaps.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child thinks two quarters make a whole, confusing half with whole.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has not understood that the cards must be arranged in a plane to cover an area, not stacked.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has confused one quarter with one whole.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically place the four cut-out fraction cards; stretch: ask them to describe a second arrangement of the four cards that also forms a whole.

exercise.description: Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Mina says she has cut a chapati in half by making one piece bigger than the other. Is she right? Write one sentence to explain your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Mina is not right. A half means two equal pieces; if one piece is bigger than the other, neither piece is a half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the two pieces match by folding one onto the other — equal parts confirm a half.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fold a paper chapati shape to show a real half first, then compare with Mina's description; stretch: ask the child to explain what Mina should do differently to get two equal halves.

exercise.description: Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Look at the four shapes below. In which shape is exactly half of the whole coloured?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle with a small sliver coloured

options.label: B
options.text: A rectangle with three of its four equal strips coloured

options.label: C
options.text: A square with exactly two of its four equal parts coloured

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle with only a tiny corner coloured

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A square with exactly two of its four equal parts coloured — two equal parts out of four equal parts is the same as one half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the coloured region and the uncoloured region are equal in size — equal parts confirm a half.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has not checked whether the coloured part equals the uncoloured part.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be counting coloured sections without comparing their size to the whole.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is guessing rather than comparing the coloured and uncoloured areas.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a copy of the shape to check which option has matching parts; stretch: ask the child to say how much is coloured in option C and name that fraction.

exercise.description: Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Ramu has one blanket. He gives half to his sister and keeps the other half himself. His friend says, 'That is not fair — your sister's half looks bigger.' Can both halves look different but still be equal? Write one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — if both pieces are truly halves, they must be equal in size; if one looks bigger, then the blanket was not divided equally and neither piece is a half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlay or fold the two pieces: equal halves match exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a paper strip to fold and check; stretch: ask the child what Ramu should do to make sure the sharing is fair.

exercise.description: Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair? Is there another fair way?

items.prompt: On a number line from 0 to 20, Rohan marks the double of 6. Priya marks half of 18. How far apart are Rohan's mark and Priya's mark?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Double of 6 is 12. Half of 18 is 9. The distance between 12 and 9 is 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each value (double of 6 = 12; half of 18 = 9), mark both on the number line, and count the gap between them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child mark 12 and 9 on a drawn number line and count the steps between them; stretch: change one number — what if Rohan marks double of 7 instead? How far apart now?

exercise.description: On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?

items.prompt: I am a number. I am more than the half of 6, and I am less than the double of 4. Which number am I?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Half of 6 is 3, double of 4 is 8. The number must be more than 3 and less than 8. Among the options, 5 satisfies both conditions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the two boundaries (half of 6 = 3; double of 4 = 8), then check which option falls strictly between them.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child found half of 6 correctly as 3 but chose a value less than it, ignoring the 'more than' condition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child found the upper boundary as 8 but chose it, ignoring that the number must be less than 8.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have doubled 8 rather than 4, or ignored the constraints entirely.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to first write 'half of 6 = ___' and 'double of 4 = ___', then mark both on a number line and look between them; stretch: ask the child to write their own two-clue puzzle using half and double.

exercise.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112
exercise.description: I have less than the double of 3 marbles and more than the half of 8 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 4, (b) 5, (c) 6 marbles.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Diya has 12 flowers. She gives half to her mother and a quarter to her brother. How many flowers does each person get? Write the numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Half of 12 is 6 — the mother gets 6 flowers. A quarter of 12 is 3 — the brother gets 3 flowers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Halve 12 for the mother's share (12 ÷ 2 = 6); halve the result again for the quarter (6 ÷ 2 = 3).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw 12 circles and physically split them first into two groups of 6, then split one group of 6 into two groups of 3; stretch: ask how many flowers Diya has left for herself after giving to mother and brother.

exercise.description: Tick the appropriate word (half/a quarter/double) to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Which of the following shapes shows three-quarters coloured?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 1 part coloured

options.label: B
options.text: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 2 parts coloured

options.label: C
options.text: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 3 parts coloured

options.label: D
options.text: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with all 4 parts coloured

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 3 parts coloured — three out of four equal parts is three-quarters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the equal parts and count the coloured parts; three out of four equal parts is three-quarters.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has confused one quarter with three-quarters.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child identified two quarters (a half) rather than three-quarters.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has confused four quarters (a whole) with three-quarters.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child colour a drawn circle divided into 4 parts step by step — 1, then 2, then 3 — and name each stage; stretch: ask how much is uncoloured when three-quarters are coloured, and what that uncoloured part is called.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Here is a rectangle divided into 4 equal parts by two lines. Two of the parts are on the left and two are on the right. Explain in one sentence how you know this rectangle shows quarters.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The rectangle is divided into four equal parts, and each part is the same size, so each part is one quarter of the whole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that all four parts are equal in size — four equal parts of a whole means each part is one quarter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fold the rectangle to check equality of parts; stretch: ask whether a rectangle divided into four unequal parts would still show quarters, and why not.

exercise.description: Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank: 9 marbles are ___ of 18 marbles.

options.label: A
options.text: a quarter

options.label: B
options.text: double

options.label: C
options.text: half

options.label: D
options.text: three-quarters

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Half — because 9 is obtained by dividing 18 into two equal parts, and 9 + 9 = 18.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has confused the relationship: double of 9 is 18, not the other way round.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has used 'a quarter' without computing what a quarter of 18 would be.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has guessed a fraction name without connecting it to the numbers.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to split 18 counters into two equal groups and count each group; stretch: ask the child to also state the double of 9 and check their two answers against each other.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8; 8 marbles are ___ of 4; 10 marbles are ___ of 5; 5 marbles are ___ of 10; 6 marbles are ___ of 12; 12 marbles are ___ of 6.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: A shape is divided into 4 equal parts. Two parts are already coloured. What fraction of the shape is coloured?

options.label: A
options.text: four quarters

options.label: B
options.text: one quarter

options.label: C
options.text: three quarters

options.label: D
options.text: two quarters

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two quarters — two of the four equal parts are coloured, so the coloured fraction is two quarters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the coloured equal parts and name the fraction: 2 coloured parts out of 4 equal parts = two quarters.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child counted one coloured part instead of two, or confused the number of coloured parts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child overcounted and named the uncoloured parts instead of the coloured parts.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child named the whole rather than the coloured portion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically colour two parts of a drawn shape divided into four and count; stretch: ask the child what fraction is NOT coloured and what another name for two quarters is.

exercise.description: Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.
